turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh gosh, sorry we're late. I went to the wrong building and the parking garage was full, I circled forever.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're here. Sit.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): And my neighbor grabbed me in the lobby. Her husband just got told he has Parkinson's, and she said ask the doctor if you might have it too.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's him, not you. Why are you here?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Right. Um. I wake up sweaty and shaky. It scares me.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): Every morning?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Pretty much. About three weeks now.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breakfast?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): I skip it. Just coffee. I'm never hungry that early and then the morning's gone and...
[SEG0010] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm her daughter, I stay with her. She takes the diabetes pills and goes right to the coffee. I've tried.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Which pills?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Metformin and, uh, gliklazide. The gliklazide is 80 milligrams in the morning. I've had the type 2 about twelve years.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Metformin dose?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): I thought it was 500 twice a day. Wait, no, sorry, it's the thousand milligram tablets, twice a day.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Morning and dinner for that one. Gliklazide just once, before the coffee.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other diabetes medicine now?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): I stopped the Jardience in March. Ten milligrams. It had me up peeing all night.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): They talked about insulin and I never took it. I won't do needles. Is that bad? Are you going to make me?
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not today. Chest pain with the shakes?
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short of breath?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ever pass out?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No, I haven't.
[SEG0025] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She did get confused once. Last Tuesday morning she couldn't tell me the day. It passed after I got some juice in her.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): I don't remember that. Was it a stroke? Am I going to get Parkinson's like her husband?
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): One episode, cleared with juice. Fits a low sugar. Not a stroke.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): So the sugar's crashing? Do I stop metformin? Is gliklazide the problem? Should I throw it out?
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Likely a low from the gliklazide on an empty stomach. Metformin stays.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): What if I'm at the store? What if I'm driving the car?
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sit down. Juice or glucose tabs. Don't drive till it settles.
[SEG0032] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I should check a number when she's sweaty?
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. Before the juice if you can.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pressure today is 136 over 74. Pulse 82.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): No tremor right now. Heart is regular. Skin's dry.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Is 136 awful? Is that a heart attack starting? Do I need a pressure pill?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not awful. No new pill.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm ordering an A1c and a fasting glucose. Lab tomorrow morning, before you eat.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Is the needle big? Will it hurt? Do I have to fast for both of them?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Small needle. Water only after midnight. Pills after the draw, with breakfast.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): What if I forget and drink coffee? I always drink coffee. I don't even think about it.
[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): Then we move the fasting test. Don't drink it.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get her there. She walks right past the toast. Every single morning.
[SEG0044] person_2 (DOCTOR): Breakfast every day. Gliclazide with food. Not on an empty stomach.
[SEG0045] person_1 (PATIENT): Are you cutting the dose today? What if the shakes don't stop? When do I see you again?
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not cutting it today. Back in two weeks with the results. If a morning sugar is under 70, call sooner.

spec.situation: Older diabetic on gliclazide and metformin with morning sweating and shakiness; skips breakfast; daughter reports confusion once; doctor reviews doses and plans a blood test.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

omissions.text: Metformin timing was specified as morning and dinner.
Gliclazide was specified to be taken once daily before coffee.
Empagliflozin/Jardiance was stopped in March because it caused nocturia/peeing all night.
Patient has never taken insulin despite discussion of starting it and stated refusal of needles.
Doctor advised metformin should be continued and not stopped.
Doctor assessed the brief confusion episode as fitting hypoglycemia and specifically not a stroke.
Doctor said there is no need to start a blood pressure medicine today.
If the patient forgets and drinks coffee, the fasting glucose test should be rescheduled/moved.
Doctor explicitly said not to cut the gliclazide dose today.

omissions.text: Patient reported the morning sweating and shakiness 'scares me.'
Caregiver stated the patient takes the diabetes pills and then goes right to coffee.
Gliclazide timing was specified as in the morning, and caregiver clarified it is taken just once before coffee.
Patient said insulin had been discussed previously but she never started it because she refuses needles and asked if the doctor was going to make her take it.

Patient was worried the confusion episode might have been a stroke and separately worried about having Parkinson's like her neighbor's husband; doctor reassured it was not a stroke and not Parkinson's.
